I'm 65 this year, been farming these same fields for 30 years. My middle school education means I can read the extension leaflets when they come around, but truthfully I rely on what I've seen with my own eyes and what the neighbors do. I have 20 mu total — not tiny, but not a big business farm either. I keep 17 mu in wheat-maize double cropping; that's my foundation, feeds the family and brings steady cash. The other 3 mu on the south edge I grow chrysanthemum — the buyer from the county medicine company comes every autumn, and if the flowers are good, the price is decent.

It's late April now. The wheat I planted last October is at jointing stage. April has been dry — we got some rain in March but not enough. The wheat is looking a bit yellow, so I'm irrigating this week, second time since spring. I'll topdress with urea at the same time, about 12 kg per mu. Last year I only did 8 kg and my yield was down to about 420 kg/mu, while my neighbor Zhang used more and got nearly 500 kg/mu. At my age, I'd rather spend a bit more on fertilizer than risk a bad year — losing 50 kg of wheat hurts more than saving 20 yuan on urea. I already put down phosphate and some compound fertilizer at planting, so now it's just nitrogen and water the wheat needs. I also spotted some aphids and a little powdery mildew on the lower leaves, so I'll spray once this week. That costs maybe 25 yuan per mu, but if I skip it, I could lose much more.

For the maize, I don't have to plant it yet, but I know the drill: as soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I have about five to seven days to get the maize in the ground. I always buy hybrid seed — I've tried saving my own seed before and the yield drop just isn't worth it. I'll buy the seed in May to be ready. I'll hire the zero-till planter from the machinery cooperative — 35 yuan per mu — because at 65 I can't turn over 17 mu by hand in a week, and my sons are busy with their factory jobs in the county. I'll put compound fertilizer down with the planter, about 30 kg per mu, and then topdress with urea around the V6 stage in July if the rain doesn't come. Two irrigations for the maize should be enough if the summer is normal.

The chrysanthemum seedlings need to go in now too — late April, early May is the right window. I got some chicken manure cheap from the poultry farm down the road, worked it into the 3 mu plot. Chrysanthemum needs a lot of hand weeding, so that's mostly family labor — my daughter-in-law and my wife handle that. I'll put down a small amount of compound fertilizer after transplanting, maybe 15 kg per mu total across the season, split twice. Chrysanthemum needs water but not flooding, so I'll irrigate by furrow four times through the summer. The main pest is caterpillars, so I keep an eye on that and spray when I see damage — usually twice.

Money is always on my mind. With seven people in the house and three grandchildren in school, even though my two sons send some money from their factory jobs, I still watch every yuan. But I've learned that being too cheap on inputs is a false economy. I'm budgeting about 500 yuan per mu for the wheat-maize system across the year, and about 400 yuan per mu for the chrysanthemum. It's a lot of cash upfront, but if I cut back, the yield惩罚 is worse than the savings.
